html:
The Ahom kingdom ruled the Brahmaputra valley of Assam for about six hundred years, from 1228 to 1826. On the 1783 and 1815 maps it is in its last, troubled decades.

The Ahoms were a Tai people who crossed the hills from upper Burma under Sukaphaa in 1228. They mixed with the valley's peoples, took up Hinduism over time and kept careful court chronicles called buranjis. Their kingdom along the Brahmaputra grew where the old Kamarupa had been.

The Ahoms held off the Mughal Empire many times, most famously at the Battle of Saraighat in 1671. But the Moamoria rebellion from 1769 tore the kingdom apart, and in 1817 Burmese armies invaded. Britain drove them out in the First Anglo-Burmese War and took Assam under the Treaty of Yandabo in 1826. Within a few years the British found wild tea here and began the plantations; see the Assam tea plant.
